centralClaim: Florida pastor Scott Winters is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT's medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for the symptoms that preceded a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.

corroboration.quote: A Florida man sued OpenAI on Wednesday, alleging ChatGPT's medical advice discouraged him from seeking treatment for symptoms that preceded a life-threatening pulmonary embolism, nearly costing him his life.

A Florida man who sought health guidance on ChatGPT sued OpenAI Wednesday, claiming the artificial intelligence chatbot gave him dangerously inaccurate medical advice that led him to delay seeking professional treatment for a pulmonary embolism.

caption:
Scott Winters, a 55 year old pastor in Florida, asked ChatGPT-4o about dizziness and blood pressure swings in 2025. His lawsuit says the chatbot told him to stay recliner bound until he had 8-10 more episodes, and that it leaned on his faith to keep him talking. Weeks later he suffered what the suit calls a massive pulmonary embolism, and doctors linked the clot to his immobility.

He is asking a San Francisco court for damages, and for ChatGPT Health to be paused until independent auditors deem it safe. One day after he filed, OpenAI began letting ChatGPT connect to Apple Health and to medical records for users in the US.

These are allegations in a complaint that has not been tested in court. OpenAI says ChatGPT is not a doctor and should never be used as a substitute for medical care, diagnosis or treatment.
